“It is becoming increasingly difficult to distinguish what is real and what isn’t online,” said Secretary Bellows. “AI and other automated tools help partisan operatives or cybercriminals create websites that look official even when they’re not. While some non-governmental sites about voting present accurate information, many do not.”

Many sites are designed to encourage citizens to register to vote and may in fact redirect visitors to official sites. However, many sites may require visitors to enter their personal information before they are redirected. Official state addresses will include .gov. For example, Mainers can register to vote at https://www.maine.gov/vote or find official election information by visiting the Secretary of State’s website at https://www.maine.gov/sos. 

“If you don’t see .gov in the web address, it is not an official state government website,” Secretary Bellows said. “If you are being asked to enter personal information like name and email address before you get to an official .gov link, then someone else is getting your private data. Instead of giving out private information to sites that might try to scam you or steal your data, go straight to the source at maine.gov/vote.”  

Secretary Bellows also encouraged voters to be careful when viewing election information on social media and always research and vet the information that they read. 

“There is unfortunately so much misinformation and disinformation out there, it can be overwhelming and difficult to know what’s true and what’s not,” said Secretary Bellows. “Everyone can play a part in reducing anxiety about the upcoming election by going to official sources and not sharing or posting unvetted and potentially false content. We have had safe, free, and secure elections in Maine for over 200 years, and we expect the same this November.”

MaineCare in Education: Updated Joint Individual Education Program (IEP) Guidance for School Health-Related Services

Sep 24, 2026

As a reminder, all providers who deliver services following the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) must ensure all MaineCare-covered services are documented following the Department of Health and Human Services/Maine Department of Education Joint IEP Guidance document. 

The Maine Department of Education has released updated Joint IEP Guidance to help schools follow federal and state requirements. The updated guidance was developed through a collaborative effort and is available on the MaineCare in Education web page. 

DOE first released the Joint Guidance on August 28, 2026, and has re-issued this guidance effective September 18, 2026. The reissued guidance replaces the previously issued Joint Guidance and provides clarification in response to questions and feedback received from School Administrative Units (SAUs), providers, and other interested parties. 

All IEP documents must reflect the updated guidance as soon as possible, but no later than thirty (30) days of the issuance of the guidance. 

Providers with current prior authorizations for School Health-Related Services through Acentra should upload any updated documentation to Atrezzo. Acentra will accept IEP language from both versions through October 18, 2026. Beginning October 19, 2026, Acentra will only accept IEP language from the new version re-issued on September 18, 2026. 

For technical assistance regarding the billing and processing of MaineCare claims, please contact your Provider Relations Specialist. 

For all other questions related to the provision of MaineCare School Health-Related Services, please contact Trista Collins, State Medicaid Educational Liaison.    

For technical information related to IEP development, please contact Dan Hemdal at the Maine Department of Education.

items.title: US Department of Labor awards $65M to develop, expand access to training opportunities through Workforce Pell Grants

Reminders in Preparation for Maine eCourts and eFiling in Cumberland County Courts

Date: 9/23/2026

On Monday, September 28, 2026, the Maine Judicial Branch is expanding Maine eCourts to all case types in Judicial Region 2, comprising Cumberland County Unified Criminal Docket (UCD), Cumberland County Superior Court, Portland District Court, and Bridgton District Court.

All case types -- civil, family, juvenile and criminal cases -- will be included in the transition from paper filing to electronic filing. As of Monday, September 28, all mandatory electronic filers pursuant to the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS) will be required to eFile documents in these courts. Self-represented litigants (parties who do not have attorneys) who file fewer than six cases in a calendar year will not be required to eFile.

Court Closures and Emergency Filing Procedures
To prepare for the implementation of Maine eCourts and eFiling on September 28, Region 2 courts are currently operating on a modified schedule and have emergency filing procedures in place. In addition, all Region 2 courts will be closed from 8 a.m. to noon the week of September 28th. Please refer to the schedule of closures and emergency procedures during these closings.

ShareFile Discontinued in Region 2 Courts
The ShareFile platform used in Region 2 courts will be disabled for all criminal, civil violation, juvenile filings, and GAL vouchers, at 2:00 p.m. on Thursday, September 24. Starting Monday, September 28, attorneys must instead use eFileMaine. Please note, attorney vouchers filed pursuant to the Standing Order regarding Payment to Court-Appointed Counsel will continue to be accepted by ShareFile for a grace period of 60 days.

Training Resources
For attorneys and staff who are new to using eFileMaine, we highly recommend viewing the recorded videos, particularly the video excerpts, available on the Maine eCourts Trainings and Resources web page. In addition to the recordings, the information and resources available on the Maine eCourts Trainings and Resources web page offer guidance for setting up your eFileMaine account and instructions to eFile documents successfully.

Personal Identifying Information (PII) Attachment (CR-CV-JV-297)
Pursuant to the Maine Rules of Electronic Court Systems (MRECS) filers are responsible for omitting or redacting nonpublic information in electronically filed documents. If the filer decides to omit rather than redact, the personal identifying information must be included on this form.

The PII form should be uploaded as an attachment to the associated filing document, in the same way that an exhibit is submitted.

Online Fine Payments
As of September 28th, parties who wish to make criminal fine payments online for cases in Cumberland County will be directed to the new online payment portal, Maine eCourts Criminal Fines and Fees. Visit Maine eCourts: Pay a Court Fine to learn more.

Support
Support for eFiling is available by emailing ecourtshelp@courts.maine.gov or by calling (207) 213-2813, Monday through Thursday from 10 a.m. to 2 p.m.

For more information on Maine eCourts and eFiling, visit: https://www.courts.maine.gov/ecourts/index.html

30 OCTOBER TERM, 2025 
Syllabus 
PUNG, PERSONAL REPRESENTATIVE OF THE 
ESTATE OF PUNG v. ISABELLA COUNTY, 
MICHIGAN 
certiorari to the united states court of appeals for 
the sixth circuit 
No. 25–95. Argued February 25, 2026—Decided June 23, 2026 
The Pung family owed $2,241.93 in real-property taxes, so local tax author-
ities in Isabella County, Michigan, initiated foreclosure proceedings and 
sold the Pung home—which was assessed at $194,400 for tax purposes— 
for $76,008 at public auction. Michael Pung sued in Federal court, and 
the District Court granted Pung partial summary judgment on his Fifth 
Amendment claim. The court held that Pung should receive only the 
surplus proceeds from the tax sale—i. e., the difference between the 
sale price and the tax debt—not the property's fair market value. The 
District Court also rejected Pung's claim under the Eighth Amendment 
Excessive Fines Clause. The Sixth Circuit affrmed. 
Held: 
1. The proper baseline for measuring “just compensation” following a 
tax sale is the auction sale price, not the property's hypothetical fair 
market value, at least when the sale is fairly conducted in light of the 
country's history of tax sales. Pp. 35–43. 
(a) For hundreds of years, English and American law have allowed 
the seizure and sale of property as a tax-collection method, provided 
that the government return any surplus proceeds to the debtor. Fed-

Maine's Minimum Wage to Increase to $15.70 Per Hour in 2027

September 18, 2026

For Immediate Release: September 18, 2026

Media Contact: Autumn Mahoney, Communications Specialist media.dol@maine.gov

AUGUSTA - The Maine Department of Labor announced today that, effective January 1, 2027, the state minimum wage will increase from $15.10 to $15.70 per hour, based on data recently made available by the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics. MDOL is required under Maine law (Maine statute Title 26, chapter 7, section 664) to make annual adjustments to the minimum wage based on the cost-of-living index (CPI-W) for the Northeast Region, after Maine voters amended the law by referendum in 2016. Between August 2025 and August 2026, there was a 4.1 percent increase in the CPI-W.

According to the U.S. Department of Labor's Bureau of Labor Statistics Current Population Survey for 2025, there were 28,000 hourly workers who were paid less than $15.00 per hour. These workers represent about four percent of all wage and salary workers (both paid at hourly rates and not paid at hourly rates) and about eight percent of wage and salary workers who are paid at hourly rates.

Agricultural workers in Maine are also entitled to the state minimum wage, after the Legislature enacted and Governor Mills signed "An Act to Establish a State Minimum Hourly Wage for Agricultural Workers" in 2025.

The "tip wage," or service employee minimum wage, will increase from $7.55 to $7.85 per hour. This means that service employees must receive a direct cash wage of at least $7.85 per hour from the employer. The employer must be able to show that the employee receives at least the minimum wage of $15.70 per hour when the direct wage and tips are combined at the end of the week. The amount of tips necessary to qualify as a service employee will increase from $191 to $199 per month.

The minimum salary threshold for exempting a worker from overtime pay must exceed 3,000 times the State's minimum wage or the annualized rate established by the U.S. Department of Labor, whichever is higher. Starting January 1, 2027, the new minimum salary threshold for salaried workers exempt from overtime will be $905.79 per week, or $47,101.08 per year. This is only one of the factors used in determining whether a worker is exempt from overtime pay under federal or state law. An individual can earn more than the minimum salary threshold and still be eligible for overtime. The duties of each worker must be considered as part of this analysis.

Employers can download the required minimum wage poster at no cost on the Department's website.

The minimum wage and overtime law can be found here.

  • The Town of Bingham will install high-efficiency heat pumps and a rooftop solar system in order to lower their energy costs at the municipally owned Veterans Building;
  • The Town of Madawaska will use their grant to launch the RIDER Program, a shared e-bike fleet in a rural community that doesn't have public transportation;

We've attracted investments in emerging industries and renewables, and we've created good-paying, green collar jobs. We've reduced our reliance on expensive fossil fuels, and we've mobilized scientists, industry leaders, local and state officials, and young people from all over to act as one to address the effects of climate change.

The messages, typically sent to a consumer’s email address, appear to come from a consumer’s financial institution, claiming that the bank or credit union is updating its online banking platform and that the consumer needs to provide verification of account information. The scammers request that the consumer click through links in the email, which direct the user to a site asking for sensitive account information. The messages threaten immediate suspension of the consumer’s access to online banking services unless the account information is provided.

The Bureau of Financial Institutions reminds consumers to look out for this scam and not to divulge bank or credit union account numbers or other personal information by email, text, or phone. The customers of several banks and credit unions received emails related to this scam, and anyone with an email account is a potential target. “Banks and credit unions will not email, text, or call customers asking them to divulge account numbers, pins, or social security numbers,” Superintendent Lloyd P. LaFountain III said.

LaFountain emphasized that customers receiving unexpected e-mails regarding online banking updates should call their bank or credit union directly and talk to an employee. Financial institution employees will be able to inform the consumer if the bank or credit union is currently updating its online banking system. The Superintendent also noted that customers should always be vigilant to protect their personal information and monitor account statements.

If a consumer suspects he or she has received a scam email, the consumer should:

  • Not click through any links in the email. Clicking the link itself may expose the consumer’s personal information to scammers and harmful software.
  • Never provide personal account information or other personal information in response to an e-mail, text, or call. A bank or credit union does not request personal account information in such a manner.
  • Be on the lookout for suspicious links. Check the “From” header in any email received – if the name of the author of the email does not match the author’s email address, this is a sign of a potential scam attempt. Another way to check suspicious links is to hover the cursor over the link without clicking the link itself – by doing this, the address for the link will appear on the consumer’s screen. If the link address shown on the screen is different from what the email says, this is a sign of a potential scam.

The Bureau of Financial Institutions has a consumer library with helpful information about how consumers can spot and avoid financial scams. Also, the Bureau’s Consumer Outreach Specialist is available to answer any consumer questions related to financial scams or accounts in general. The Bureau’s phone number is 207-624-8570.

items.title: Secretary of State marks Constitution Day with unveiling of official printing of Maine Constitution
items.content_text:
First printing since 1876 includes redacted indigenous treaty obligations
AUGUSTA, MAINE
– Secretary of State Shenna Bellows marked Constitution Day by formally unveiling the official printing of the Maine Constitution, the first formal printing since 1876. The unveiling took place at the Maine State Cultural Center in Augusta and included displays of the original 1820 copy of the Maine State Constitution and the 1876 version along with the new printing.
For more than a century, Maine omitted three original sections – Sections 1, 2 and 5, of Article X of the Constitution – from official printed copies. The sections, which remained in full force despite the redaction, include treaty obligations to the Wabanaki tribal nations. In 2023, Mainers voted overwhelmingly to cancel the 1876 amendment compelling the redaction and restore the language to printed copies of the constitution.
“Restoring this language to the Maine Constitution is a visible and lasting reminder of the important role the Wabanaki people played in the formation of Maine,” said Secretary Bellows. “The Wabanaki have existed in Maine for 13,000 years, and voters made it clear that their immeasurable contributions to our collective past, present and future should be known, acknowledged and celebrated, not hidden from history.”
The large format version was printed using a 19th century letterpress onto vellum by Wolfe Editions of Portland and will be permanently housed at the Maine State Archives along with the previous versions.

Measles is a highly contagious viral disease. If one person has measles, 90% of the people close to that person who are not immune will become infected. Symptoms of measles include:

  • Fever
  • Cough
  • Runny nose
  • Red, watery eyes
  • Rash that spreads from the head down.

Individuals who develop symptoms should contact their health care provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection. If symptoms are consistent with measles, a health care professional may test to determine a measles infection.

Measles can cause severe sickness including pneumonia, encephalitis (brain swelling), and death. An infected person spreads measles through coughs or sneezes. Once infected, a person is contagious from four days before their rash starts through four days afterwards. The virus remains alive for up to two hours on surfaces and in the air. The period from exposure to onset of symptoms is typically 10 to 14 days, but can be longer.

The measles, mumps, and rubella (MMR) vaccine is the best prevention for measles. Individuals who:   

  • have been potentially exposed should review their vaccine history and watch for symptoms.
  • are not immunized or do not know their measles immunization status should get vaccinated.
  • develop symptoms should contact their health provider for instructions before going to the provider’s office or hospital. This will help prevent the spread of further infection.

Recommendations: 

  • Children – Identify and vaccinate children who are not up to date with their MMR vaccines. All children should receive two doses of MMR vaccine. A health care professional should administer the first dose to children at 12 to 15 months old and the second at 4 to 6 years old.
    • Children 6 to 11 months old who will be traveling internationally or domestically to a region with a known active measles outbreak should receive one dose of MMR vaccine, per the Maine CDC’s expanded recommendations for those traveling to a destination with a known outbreak. This dose is not considered part of the routine two-dose series starting at age 12 months.  
  • Adults – All adults should have proof of immunity to measles. Acceptable proof includes one of the following:
    • written documentation of vaccination
    • laboratory evidence of immunity
    • birth before 1957
    • or laboratory confirmation of disease
    • individuals who received a measles vaccine between 1963 to 1967 are encouraged to speak with their doctor to determine if additional vaccination is needed. Those known to have received an inactivated dose measles vaccine should receive a single dose of MMR. Five percent of people who received measles vaccine between 1963 and 1967 received an inactivated vaccine.

For adults with no evidence of immunity to measles, the U.S. CDC recommends one dose of MMR vaccine as soon as possible. Adults who are traveling domestically or internationally to a region known to have an active measles outbreak should receive two doses of the vaccine. Pregnant women should not receive any live virus vaccine during pregnancy, including MMR.

Vaccination Information:

  • Two doses of MMR vaccine are about 97% effective at preventing measles; one dose is about 93% effective.
  • The U.S. CDC considers people who received two doses of MMR vaccine as a child protected for life. 
  • Some people exposed to the virus may still get measles even if they got the MMR vaccine. In this case, they are more likely to have a milder illness and are also less likely to spread the disease to other people.

  • The Maine CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.maine.gov/dhhs/measles
  • The U.S. CDC’s measles webpage: http://www.cdc.gov/measles/index.html
  • The Maine Immunization Program webpage: https://www.maine.gov/dhhs/mecdc/infectious-disease/immunization/

items.title: Digital Archives
items.content_text:
Welcome to the online digital collection of the Maine State Archives, a bureau within the Department of the Secretary of State. We maintain approximately 8 miles of official state records (both paper and digital) that are deemed permanently valuable. These records include bills introduced in the Legislature, reports from the Governor's Executive Council, election returns, deeds and maps from the Maine Land Office, vital statistics prior to 1892, federal census records up to 1880, county court records dating back to 1636, and military records through World War I, among others.
As of March 1, 2026, our online collection includes over one million individual records. The Maine State Archives will continue to expand this database as we digitize more of our collection. All documents are public records and are free to download. To begin your search, check the following sources:
Digital Archives Portal
: Open Access - online digital collection of the Maine State Archives.
ArchivesSpace Public Interface
: Use this database to search through the archival findings aids, collection structures, and descriptions of physical and digital records managed by the bureau.
Maine Memory Network
: A digital history platform featuring specific exhibits, historical photographs, and selected primary documents contributed by the Maine State Archives.
Family Search
: FamilySearch is the world’s largest free genealogy resource.

items.title: Maine Needham Day - September 26
items.content_text:
WHEREAS
, the Maine Needham was first introduced in 1872 by John Seavey, owner of the confectionary Seavey’s Sweets, which is rumored to have been located in either Auburn or Portland at the time; and
WHEREAS
, named after a popular preacher of that era, George C. Needham, the Needham candy consists of a mashed potato center surrounded by coconut and chocolate; and
WHEREAS
, it is thought that Needhams gained popularity with home cooks during the Great Depression, when Maine people would use their extra potato harvest to make the treat; and
WHEREAS
, Needhams have become synonymous with Maine, and they help celebrate locally harvested Maine potatoes; and
WHEREAS
, today, sweet shops and home cooks around our state keep the beloved tradition of the Needham alive by continuing to produce and perfect this iconic Maine treat for us to enjoy and share with the world; and
WHEREAS
, on September 26, 2026 the fourth annual Maine Needham Festival will be held at the Maine Tasting Center in Wiscasset to celebrate the Needham and it’s great history in Maine; and
WHEREAS
, in accordance with 1 MRSA § 150-S, the State of Maine observes the last Saturday in September each year as Maine Needham Day;
NOW THEREFORE
, be it resolved that I, Janet T. Mills, Governor of the State of Maine, do hereby proclaim September 26, 2026 as
Maine Needham Day
and I urge all citizens to recognize the Needham’s history and celebrate this delectable Maine treat.
In testimony whereof, I have caused
the Great Seal of the State to be
hereunto affixed GIVEN under my
hand at Augusta this tenth day
of September Two Thousand Twenty-Six

items.title: US Supreme Court Upholds Right to Vote by Mail
items.content_text:
AUGUSTA, MAINE
– Absentee voting by mail will continue just as it has in prior elections, announced Secretary of State Shenna Bellows today.  The US Supreme Court rejected the US Postal Service and Trump Administration’s quest to change the rules for mailed ballots.  States including the State of Maine had filed a lawsuit to challenge the Trump Executive Order and US Postal Service rule that would have dramatically limited the ability of clerks to mail ballots to voters.  A lower court blocked the rule on constitutional grounds, and the US Supreme Court denied the Trump Administration’s attempt to overturn the lower court.
“This is good news for voters and for democracy.  Voters can rest assured that they have all of the same options for absentee voting including receiving and returning their ballot by mail that they have had in every other election,” said Secretary of State Shenna Bellows.  “We know that many Mainers – particularly seniors and people with disabilities – appreciate the convenience of voting from home, and we are thrilled that our joint legal efforts with states across the country to protect the right to vote by mail have succeeded.”
Voters can request absentee ballots utilizing the Secretary of State’s online
absentee ballot portal
, in writing, or by calling their
municipal clerk
directly. Absentee voting in Maine begins October 5, and voters should start receiving their ballots in the mail in the first week of October. Voters can track the status of their absentee ballot via Maine’s
online absentee ballot tracking portal
.
